traveler: María Pita (Mayor Fernández da Cámara Pita)
title: The Breach and the Petition: a Butcher's Widow at the Wall of A Coruña and at the Court of Two Kings
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: A Coruña, the shop in the Peixería
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the marriage (Saavedra Vázquez, via Briante Benítez 2020 p.104); month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Simón Arnao and María Pita, called la vieja, marry and keep a shop in the Peixería, the fishermen's quarter that spreads below the walled town of A Coruña. The quarter lies outside the wall, undefended, the first thing any enemy coming in off the sea would reach, and thirty-five years from this marriage English troops will burn it to its foundations. Their daughter will be christened Mayor Fernández da Cámara Pita, and in her youth she works at that counter. The family sells; it does not govern.
suggested_refs: The Pescadería quarter of A Coruña, outside the wall of the Cidade Vella
sources: Saavedra Vázquez, cited in Briante Benítez, 'María Pita en el teatro,' Madrygal 23 (2020), p.104
María del Carmen Saavedra Vázquez, María Pita. Una aproximación a su vida y a su tiempo (A Coruña: Vía Láctea, 2003)

stops.name: A Coruña, a birth with two dates and two places
stops.date_confidence: contested and unresolved. Saavedra Vázquez argues from the archive for c.1556; Martínez Salazar, the first biographer, gives 1562-1568 and puts the birth not in A Coruña but at Sigrás, in Cambre, a reading López Rodríguez (2023) p.172 endorses. Popular tradition says 1565. No baptismal entry has been located in any of these parishes. The pin follows the Saavedra/Briante reading; the year and the place are both open
stops.campa: The child is born, and the record does not agree on when or where. Saavedra Vázquez reads the archive to about 1556; Andrés Martínez Salazar, the first man who went looking, puts the birth between 1562 and 1568 and puts it at Sigrás in the parish of Cambre, inland, where the woman will in fact die. Popular memory settles on 1565 because a round number is easier to carry. Her origin in the old town is inferred from where her parents kept their shop and from nothing else. No baptismal entry has been produced by anyone who has searched.
suggested_refs: The parish registers of the Cidade Vella and of Santiago de Sigrás, searched without result for a baptism
sources: Saavedra Vázquez, María Pita. Una aproximación a su vida y a su tiempo, p.27
Andrés Martínez Salazar, El cerco de La Coruña en 1589 (1988 ed.), pp.116, 129
López Rodríguez, Anales del Instituto de Estudios Madrileños LXIII (2023), pp.156, 172

stops.name: A Coruña, the house on the Rúa das Herrerías
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year (López Rodríguez 2023 pp.158-159, after Martínez Salazar); month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: She marries Juan Alonso de Rois, a butcher of San Cristóbal das Viñas, and a daughter is born to them, María Alonso de Rois, who will one day rename herself María Alonso de Pita after her mother. The house on the Rúa das Herrerías, number 24 in the old street numbering and 28 in the new, is one of three addresses the documents give her; the others are Santa María 26, formerly the Carnicería, and Cortaduría 9. Butchers' streets, all of them. The trade she marries into is meat.
suggested_refs: The Casa Museo María Pita, Rúa das Herrerías 28, A Coruña
sources: López Rodríguez (2023), pp.157-159, citing Martínez Salazar 1988
es.wikipedia.org, 'María Pita' (for the attribution of the house to Rois, which rests on Wikipedia alone)

stops.name: A Coruña, the death of María Pita la vieja
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year (Saavedra Vázquez 2011 pp.38-39, via Briante Benítez 2020 p.109); month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Her mother dies, and what passes to the daughter is not the shop but the name. María Pita is the short form of it: she will sign that to the King of Spain, an unrelated lawsuit will find it already set to verse in Galician while she is alive to hear it, and a city will eventually carve it at nine metres of bronze and granite in front of its town hall. But Mayor Fernández da Cámara Pita is what the notaries write on every instrument she is party to, and it is what the parish will write over her burial sixty years from now.
suggested_refs: The Pescadería shop of Simón Arnao and María Pita la vieja
sources: Saavedra Vázquez 2011, pp.38-39, cited in Briante Benítez, Madrygal 23 (2020), p.109

stops.name: A Coruña, the first widowhood and the suit against a son-in-law
stops.date_confidence: the death of Juan Alonso de Rois is dated 1587 by López Rodríguez (2023) p.157; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Briante says only that she was widowed after a few years. The figure of c.1585 that circulates in the lens material is not supported by either scholar
stops.campa: Juan Alonso de Rois dies. His widow does not withdraw into mourning; she goes to law. An inheritance from Elena de Rois, her dead husband's grandmother, has ended up in the hands of Gregorio Vázquez de Verbía, who is married to her own daughter. She sues him for it and comes out of the case holding lands and property. Nothing in the file suggests the family connection slowed her down, and nothing in the fifty years afterwards suggests she thought it should. It is the first suit the record shows. The defendant is her son-in-law.
suggested_refs: The Elena de Rois inheritance case against Gregorio Vázquez de Verbía
sources: López Rodríguez (2023), pp.157-159, citing Martínez Salazar 1988

stops.name: A Coruña, the second marriage
stops.date_confidence: the two scholars conflict and are not reconciled here. López Rodríguez (2023) p.157: the second wedding took place in November 1587. Briante Benítez (2020) p.105: she remarried before July 1587. The pin date follows López; the day is unknown and defaulted to 01
stops.campa: She marries Gregorio de Rocamonde, another butcher, in the same year she buried the first husband. The marriage has less than two years to run: Rocamonde will be killed on the wall of his own city in May of 1589, by men who came in off the sea. The two scholars who have printed the archive cannot be made to agree on the month of the wedding. López Rodríguez has it in November of 1587; Briante Benítez has her remarried already before July of the same year. Both cannot be right, and neither has answered the other.
suggested_refs: The marriage record of Mayor Fernández Pita and Gregorio de Rocamonde, 1587

segments.name: The Fleet Off the Point: May 1589

stops.name: A Coruña, the fleet stands in
stops.date_confidence: attested (Briante Benítez 2020 p.110, following Saavedra Vázquez 1989, 2003, 2011, and the contemporary diary of Captain Juan Varela)
stops.campa: On the fourth of May a fleet stands in off A Coruña: between a hundred and eighty and two hundred sail under Francis Drake and Sir John Norris, five to six thousand troops aboard, sent out to answer the Armada of the year before. The city has a walled old town on the height and, below it, the open Pescadería where the fish are sold and where the Pita family has kept a shop for thirty-five years. The garrison is small. The wall runs where it runs, and the Pescadería is outside it.
suggested_refs: The 1589 Drake-Norris expedition, the English Armada
sources: Saavedra Vázquez, cited ibid.; contemporary diary of Capt. Juan Varela

stops.name: Santa María de Oza, the landing
stops.date_confidence: the landing at the beach of Santa María de Oza is attested (Briante Benítez 2020 p.110); the exact day within 4-6 May is not fixed in the sources consulted
stops.campa: The English put men ashore at the beach of Santa María de Oza, east of the town and out of reach of the harbour guns, and march on the city overland. There is no battle at the water's edge. By nightfall the shape of the siege is set: an army on the land side, a fleet in the bay, and a town whose defenders are its garrison, its councillors, its fishermen and its women, with no relief force anywhere in Galicia that can reach it in time. From the sand to the wall is under three miles.
suggested_refs: The beach of Santa María de Oza, landing ground of the English force
sources: Briante Benítez, Madrygal 23 (2020), p.110, citing Saavedra Vázquez

stops.name: A Coruña, the Pescadería taken
stops.date_confidence: attested that the lightly fortified Pescadería fell to the English in the opening days of the siege (Briante Benítez 2020 p.110); the precise day is not given, and 6 May is an ordering date
stops.campa: The Pescadería falls first because it was never defensible. The English take the quarter of the shops, the drying racks and the fish stalls, and the defenders pull back behind the wall of the Cidade Vella with what they can carry. What is left to hold is the high town, its cisterns, its churches and a wall built for a smaller kind of war than the one that has arrived. The house she was raised in and the counter she worked at stand inside the enemy's lines within two days of the landing.
suggested_refs: The burning of the Pescadería, May 1589

stops.name: Convento de Santo Domingo, the English gun in the cloister
stops.date_confidence: attested (López Rodríguez 2023, p.173: the English established a firing position in the convent of Santo Domingo on 7 May 1589)
stops.campa: On the seventh of May the English set up a firing position in the convent of the Dominicans and shoot into the old town from it. The building is a church, a cloister and a burial ground for the families of A Coruña, and for the week that follows it is a redoubt. Fifty-four years from now Mayor Fernández Pita will dictate a will asking to be buried in this convent, beside her fourth husband. The parish that holds her body will not send it, and no grave of hers has been identified here or anywhere else.
suggested_refs: The convent of Santo Domingo, A Coruña, used as an English battery position, 7 May 1589

stops.name: Porta de Aires, the mine and the breach
stops.date_confidence: attested (Briante Benítez 2020 p.106; López Rodríguez 2023 p.154). The date of 3 May that circulates through Spanish Wikipedia is out of step with both scholars and is not used here
stops.campa: On the fourteenth the English fire a mine under the wall, bring down a section of it and come through the gap. Gregorio de Rocamonde is killed in the fighting there, in front of his wife. The breach is the crisis of the whole siege: if the assault carries the wall the town is lost, and the men holding the rubble are being pushed back off it. Rocamonde is one of the dead by name. How many others fall at the gap beside him is not given in any account of the siege that survives.
suggested_refs: The Porta de Aires sector of the A Coruña wall, mined and breached on 14 May 1589

stops.name: The breach, the pike and the ensign's flag
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The individual feat is absent from the surviving official documentation of the siege, per Saavedra Vázquez, and appears in her own later petitions and in narrative retellings. The passage quoted here is offered in the secondary literature as a period chronicle, but its citation trail in López Rodríguez (2023) p.154 leads to a modern blog retelling, not to an identified sixteenth or seventeenth-century document
stops.campa: An English ensign climbs the rubble with his colours, calling his men up after him, and the defenders give ground. A woman comes forward out of them with a pike, strikes him down dead and takes the flag out of his hands, and the defenders turn and hold the gap. This is the scene, and it is told in accounts written after the fact and in none written during it. What the woman herself will tell the King of Spain seven years from now is shorter and much larger: that she fought manfully, and that she killed the General of the English.
stops.quote: Adelantose entonces a la brecha un alferez enemigo, animando con la voz y el ejemplo a los suyos para que avanzasen, poniendo con ello en grave apuro a los sitiados... En tan apurado y triste momento, una mujer, llamada Maria Fernandez de la Camara y Pita, se presenta y adelanta a los defensores armada de una pica, y dirigiendose al alferez ingles le descargo un golpe tan certero que le derribo muerto, apoderandose en el acto de su bandera.
stops.quote_source: Narrative passage cited in López Rodríguez (2023), p.154, as reflecting 'las crónicas de la época' but footnoted to a modern retelling rather than to a named contemporary chronicle
suggested_refs: Saavedra Vázquez on the absence of the individual feat from the official siege record
sources: Saavedra Vázquez, María Pita. Una aproximación a su vida y a su tiempo

stops.name: The wall, the women filling the gap
stops.date_confidence: attested as a fact of the siege by the Cofradía de San Andrés testimony of 25 September 1589; Briante Benítez (2020) p.106 places the wall-reinforcement work at the point of the 14 May breach. The single day is an ordering date for work that ran through the siege
stops.campa: The wall has to be filled where the mine took it out, and the work is done by the women of the town, hauling earth and stone into the gap under fire while the fighting goes on inside it. They have been carrying food and water up to the defenders since the fleet appeared. The one contemporary document about women at A Coruña in 1589 describes them throughout in the plural. Some are killed at the rampart, among them a servant of Juan Jaspe and a shoemaker's wife, and the ones beside them do not go back down.
suggested_refs: The rampart works of the Cidade Vella, filled by the women of A Coruña during the siege
sources: Archivo General de Galicia, P. sig. 16-nº I, quoted in López Rodríguez (2023), pp.154-155

stops.name: A Coruña, the English sail for Lisbon
stops.date_confidence: attested (Briante Benítez 2020 pp.110-111, citing Saavedra Vázquez 1989, 2003, 2011)
stops.campa: On the nineteenth the English give up the town and put back to sea, standing south for Lisbon, where the rest of the expedition will fail as well. They have burned the Pescadería, killed a share of the townspeople and taken nothing they came for. A Coruña has held. Then the counting begins: the dead, the burned houses, the widows. Mayor Fernández Pita is a widow for the second time in six years. She has a daughter of the first marriage to keep, and the quarter she was raised in is ash.
suggested_refs: The English Armada of 1589 and its failure at Lisbon

stops.name: A Coruña, the mareantes testify
stops.date_confidence: attested, document dated (Archivo General de Galicia, P. sig. 16-nº I, 25 September 1589)
stops.campa: Four months after the fleet leaves, the seamen of the Cofradía de San Andrés give sworn testimony about what was done in the defence, and their statement is about women in the plural. It names no heroine. It says that many of them fought manfully, encouraging their husbands and the soldiers; that the enemy killed some of them while they were filling the towers with earth and defending the wall; and that the killing did not break the rest. The single feat at the breach is not in it.
stops.quote: las dichas mujeres fueron de mucha importancia muchas dellas peleando baronilmente anymando a los maridos y a los soldados y algunas dellas los enemigos las mataron hestando terre-plenando los cubos y defendiendo la dicha muralla... e aunque mataban algunas dellas no por eso las otras perdian el animo antes cada vez se demostraban con mas anymo y acudian con mas cuidado a la defensa de la dicha ciudad.
stops.quote_source: Testimony of the mareantes of the Cofradía de San Andrés, 25 September 1589, Archivo General de Galicia, P. sig. 16-nº I, quoted in López Rodríguez (2023), pp.154-155
suggested_refs: The Cofradía de San Andrés of A Coruña and its 1589 deposition on the women of the siege
sources: Archivo General de Galicia, P. sig. 16-nº I

segments.name: The Third Widowhood and the Captain in the House

stops.name: A Coruña, the third marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, months after the siege (Briante Benítez 2020 p.106, 111); month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Months after the siege she marries a third time, to Sancho de Arratia, and a daughter, Francisca de Arratia, comes of it and is still being named in a legal instrument thirty years later. What Arratia was is not agreed. Briante Benítez calls him an hidalgo and an officer of the navy; López Rodríguez calls him a captain of infantry in the garrison. Neither of them makes him a shipmaster out of Sanlúcar de Barrameda hauling timber to Ferrol, a detail that has attached itself to him from somewhere outside the scholarship.
suggested_refs: The 1620 legal instrument naming Francisca de Arratia

stops.name: A Coruña, widowed a third time
stops.date_confidence: attested to a window, not a day: Briante Benítez (2020) p.111 places Arratia's death between May and November 1592. August is a midpoint used to order the segment
stops.campa: The third husband dies between May and November of 1592. She is a widow for the third time, with daughters of two marriages, no husband's trade standing behind her, in a city that was sacked and half burned three years ago and has not been rebuilt. What she has instead is paper: the certificates and informes of what she did at the breach, gathered up and kept. In the Spain of Philip II a service to the crown is a form of property, and hers is written down and in her own hands.
suggested_refs: The certifications of siege service carried later to Madrid
sources: López Rodríguez (2023), p.159, citing Saavedra Vázquez pp.145-146

stops.name: A Coruña, the sentence of the Licenciado Haro
stops.date_confidence: the sentencia itself is undated in the transcription; it is placed before 1596 because the royal redress she obtains in July 1596 answers it. The 1595 date is an ordering device, not a document date
stops.campa: Captain Francisco de Peralta is quartered on her house, and the quarrel over it reaches the court. The sentence, signed by the Licenciado Haro, banishes her from A Coruña and its jurisdiction for two full years and fines her four thousand maravedís, to be paid before she is let out of the prison she is already in. Seven years after the breach, the woman of the breach is a convict of the same city. The document carries no date. It is placed here because of what she does immediately afterwards.
stops.quote: Vistos: Fallo atento le procesado que debo de condenar y condepno a la dicha Mayor Fernandez Pita a que dentro de tercero dia que como salga de la carcel y prision en questa salga desterrada y por esta mi sentencia la destierro desta ciudad, su termino y jurisdiccion por tiempo y espacio de dos anos precisos y mas en pena de quatro mill maravedis para los estrados de mi audiencia los quales de y pague antes que sea suelta de la carcel y prision en questa = Licenciado Haro = Rubrica.
stops.quote_source: Sentencia against Mayor Fernández Pita, transcribed in Martínez Salazar, El cerco de La Coruña en 1589 (1988 ed.), pp.142-201, quoted in López Rodríguez (2023), p.158
suggested_refs: The Peralta billeting file in the papers of the Real Audiencia de Galicia

stops.name: Madrid, the first arrival at court
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month (López Rodríguez 2023 p.159, citing Saavedra Vázquez pp.145-146); the day is unknown and defaulted to 01
stops.campa: She comes to Madrid for the first time, six hundred kilometres from the Peixería, carrying her documentation: informes, certifications, the sworn statements of what she did when the English came through the wall. The court of Philip II runs on exactly this, petitions out of the provinces waiting on secretaries and councils. She is a butcher's widow from Galicia, she has no patron here, and she has come to stand in the antechambers with everybody else. Most of the men in them wait years and go home with nothing.
suggested_refs: The Consejo de Cámara de Castilla and the machinery of the mercedes petition
sources: Saavedra Vázquez, María Pita. Una aproximación a su vida y a su tiempo, pp.145-146

stops.name: Madrid, the memorial to Philip II
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the document is undated within 1596, and the month here is an ordering device. Contradiction flagged and not resolved: the claim to have killed the English general is her own petition language and is absent from the surviving official siege documentation per Saavedra Vázquez
stops.campa: The memorial goes in to the King. It is written in the third person, as memorials are, and it says three things. That she went in her own person to fight, and fought manfully, so that she killed the General of the English. That she spent and gave much of her property: food, cord, bullets, every kind of munition, mattresses. That her husband was killed there and left her two unmarried daughters. She asks a licence to export two thousand mules to marry them off. Three hundred will be granted.
stops.quote: Mayor Fernandez de Camara, viuda, mujer que fue de Gregorio de Rocamonde, vezinos de la ciudad de La Coruna, dice que quando el asalto de La Coruna de los enemigos, ella fue por su persona a pelear y peleo varonilmente, de manera que mato al General de la Inglesa y gasto y dio mucha hazienda, aasi de comida, cuerdas, balas y todo genero de municion, y colchones, con otra mucha hazienda. Y alli le mataron a su marido, de quien le quedaron dos hijas doncellas.
stops.quote_source: Memorial of Mayor Fernández Pita to Philip II, 1596, Archivo General de Simancas, Cámara de Castilla, leg. 772, transcribed in López Rodríguez (2023), p.162
suggested_refs: AGS, Cámara de Castilla, legajo 772
sources: AGS, CC, leg. 772, transcribed in López Rodríguez (2023), p.162
Saavedra Vázquez, on the absence of the feat from the official siege record

stops.name: Madrid, the cédula against the captain
stops.date_confidence: attested, document dated 24 July 1596 (AGS, cited via Saavedra Vázquez p.146, quoted in López Rodríguez 2023 p.163)
stops.campa: A royal cédula orders the Captain General of Galicia to redress the grievances Captain Peralta has committed against her, and confirms that no soldier is to be quartered in her house again, in recognition of her services at the siege. The exemption is small and it is exact: her own door, in her own street, shut to the army. She will spend the next twelve years trying to get two successive governors of Galicia to enforce it. The paper is dated at Madrid, the twenty-fourth of July.
suggested_refs: The royal cédula of 24 July 1596 exempting her house from billeting
sources: Saavedra Vázquez, María Pita. Una aproximación a su vida y a su tiempo, p.146

stops.name: Madrid, three hundred mules
stops.date_confidence: attested, document dated 4 September 1596 (AGS, CC, leg. 794, referenced in López Rodríguez 2023, pp.159-160)
stops.campa: Mules move armies, mills, ore and everything else in Castile, and the crown controls how many leave the kingdom. In September she is granted a licence to take three hundred mules and mule-foals out of Galicia into Portugal, in remuneration of her services and of the loss of her husband and her property. She had asked for two thousand. A licence is not money; it is a thing that can be sold to men who have money. She will be renewing this one, and petitioning on it, for the next ten years.
suggested_refs: AGS, Cámara de Castilla, legajo 794, the mule-export licences
sources: AGS, CC, leg. 794, referenced in López Rodríguez (2023), pp.159-160

stops.name: San Lorenzo de El Escorial, two hundred more
stops.date_confidence: attested, document dated 28 October 1596 at San Lorenzo (AGS, CC, leg. 794; López Rodríguez 2023, p.160)
stops.campa: At San Lorenzo, in the granite monastery-palace Philip II raised for himself in the sierra above Madrid, a supplementary licence is signed for two hundred more head. She now holds a royal concession for five hundred mules. The paper is dated at the place where the King spends his last years among his relics and his plans, forty kilometres out from the court, and her name is entered in his registers alongside the business of an empire. Two years ago she was in prison in A Coruña under sentence of exile.
suggested_refs: The Monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial, where the supplementary licence was signed

stops.name: Madrid, the formula hardens
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year (AGS, CC, leg. 794, transcribed in López Rodríguez 2023 pp.159-160); month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: She petitions again on the licence, reciting the grounds the way the clerks require them: that His Majesty did her the favour of permission to take five hundred mules and mule-foals from the Kingdom of Galicia to Portugal, in remuneration of the services she had done and the harm she had received in the siege of the said city, her husband having been killed in it and all her property burned and carried off. That is the whole of the claim, and the wording of it barely changes over the next ten years of petitions.
stops.quote: Mayor Fernandez de Camara, vezina de la ciudad de La Coruna, dize que Vuestra Magestad le hico merced de licencia para sacar del Reyno de Galicia al de Portugal 500 mulas y muletos, en remuneracion de los servicios quella avia hecho y dano que avia recivido en el cerco de la dicha ciudad por averle muerto en ella su marido y quemado y llevado toda la hazienda.
stops.quote_source: Petition of Mayor Fernández Pita, 1597, Archivo General de Simancas, Cámara de Castilla, leg. 794, transcribed in López Rodríguez (2023), pp.159-160
suggested_refs: AGS, Cámara de Castilla, legajo 794
sources: AGS, CC, leg. 794, transcribed in López Rodríguez (2023), pp.159-160

segments.name: A New King, the Same Siege

stops.name: A Coruña, the fourth marriage
stops.date_confidence: contested year, not resolved: Briante Benítez (2020) p.106 gives 1598, López Rodríguez (2023) p.157 gives 1599. The stop takes the earlier date; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: She marries for the fourth and last time, to Gil Bermúdez de Figueroa, an escudero of the Real Audiencia de Galicia holding land at Ledoño and at San Pedro de Nos. Briante Benítez dates the wedding 1598 and López Rodríguez 1599, and the two are not reconciled. Two sons come of it, Juan and Francisco Pita de Figueroa, who carry her name as well as his. Gil's will, when it is made, provides that if she remarries she loses the tutorship of his children and the use of everything the marriage has accumulated.
suggested_refs: The testament of Gil Bermúdez de Figueroa and its remarriage clause

stops.name: Madrid, the licence renewed under the old king
stops.date_confidence: attested, document dated 30 May 1598 (AGS, CC, leg. 934, cited in López Rodríguez 2023, p.166)
stops.campa: The mule licence is renewed at Madrid in May, registered in the Cámara de Castilla, legajo 934. Philip II has four months to live. The woman who has been at his court on and off for two years, and who told him in writing that she killed the general of the English, will shortly begin again with his son, from the beginning, with the same folder of certificates and the same fortnight in May of 1589 at the middle of it. The renewal is dated at Madrid, the thirtieth of May, 1598.
suggested_refs: AGS, Cámara de Castilla, legajo 934
sources: AGS, CC, leg. 934, cited in López Rodríguez (2023), p.166

stops.name: Madrid, the pike and the morrión before Philip III
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year (AGS, CC, leg. 901, transcribed in López Rodríguez 2023 pp.163-164); month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Tagged as reconstruction on the substance: the document combines the combat claim and the supply claim without distinguishing them, and the combat claim remains uncorroborated by the siege record
stops.campa: Before the new king she tells it again, and this time the equipment is named: that she fought among the soldiers with pike and morrión, and that she furnished cloth, cord and provisions out of her own house. The two figures sit in one document, the woman in a helmet on the rubble and the woman supplying a garrison out of her stores, and the petition does not treat them as different claims. She asks aid for her children, and the office of alguacil mayor of Betanzos, to be held for a daughter's benefit.
suggested_refs: AGS, Cámara de Castilla, legajo 901
sources: AGS, CC, leg. 901, transcribed in López Rodríguez (2023), pp.163-164

stops.name: Madrid, five escudos a month and what happens to them after
stops.date_confidence: the day and month are the document's own, 15 July; the year is not secure. López Rodríguez places the petition in his 1596 narrative, but its text speaks of Philip II as the king 'que esta en el cielo', and Philip II died 13 September 1598, so it cannot be 1596. 1599 is the earliest possible July and is used to order the segment. Source is Martínez Salazar 1988 pp.122-123, not AGS CC 917 as sometimes cited
stops.campa: To the Council of War she puts the arithmetic of her position. She has five escudos a month for what she did at the wall. She asks that it be raised; that it pass to her daughters after her; and that her two young sons be given places in the infantry of A Coruña. A stipend that dies with the holder is charity. A stipend that descends is an estate, and it is an estate she is asking for. The petition is dated the fifteenth of July, and speaks of Philip II as the king who is in heaven.
suggested_refs: Martínez Salazar, El cerco de La Coruña en 1589 (1988 ed.), pp.122-123
sources: Martínez Salazar 1988, pp.122-123, quoted in López Rodríguez (2023), pp.162-163

stops.name: Madrid, Peralta ten years on
stops.date_confidence: the copy of the memorial is headed as seen on 17 August 1606, and the document's own text dates the abuses to 1596, not 1589. Flagged and unresolved: López Rodríguez prints the same memorial twice, at p.160 under 1606 and at p.164 under 17 August 1596
stops.campa: Ten years after the cédula, the Peralta case is still open, and a fresh memorial goes to the Council of War. Peralta, she says, gave her very bad treatment in deed and in word, carried off all her movable goods, broke open her chests and coffers, and, being a rich man with a long hand in the courts, arranged that the papers and informations she had drawn up against him should be stolen and hidden. The council writes on the back of it that the cédula is to be kept, and that the count is to be asked why he has not kept it.
stops.quote: Senor Mayor fernandez de camara pita vecina do la ciudad de la coruna dice que por el ano pasado de mill quinientos y nouenta y seis el capitan francisco de peralta la dio muy malos tratamientos ansi de obra como de palabra y demas desto me lleno todos mis bienes muebles y abrio las arcas y cofres y de todo esto di quenta a vtra. mag.d en su rreal consejo de guerra destos agravios... el dho. capitan por ser hombre rrico y tener mucha mano con la justicia tubo horden de hurtar y ocultar los papeles e ynformaciones que contra el auia yo echo.
stops.quote_source: Copia de un memorial de Mayor Fernández de la Cámara y Pita, sobre los malos tratamientos que la hizo el Capitán Francisco de Peralta, seen 17 August 1606, AGS, Secretaría de Guerra, leg. 660, transcribed in López Rodríguez (2023), p.160
suggested_refs: AGS, Secretaría de Guerra, legajo 660
sources: AGS, Secretaría de Guerra, leg. 660, transcribed in López Rodríguez (2023), pp.160, 164-165

stops.name: San Lorenzo de El Escorial, the licence prorogued
stops.date_confidence: attested, document dated 26 August 1606 at San Lorenzo (AGS, CC, leg. 934, transcribed in López Rodríguez 2023, pp.166-167)
stops.campa: Nine days later, at San Lorenzo again, the mule licence is prorogued two further years, two hundred head and three hundred head, under the signature of the new king. Seventeen years after the siege, the breach in the wall of A Coruña is still generating paper in the sierra above Madrid. The transaction is ordinary: a service performed, a grant made, a grant expiring, a grant renewed, and a widow at court to see that the renewal happens. The legajo is Cámara de Castilla 934, as before.
suggested_refs: AGS, Cámara de Castilla, legajo 934, prorogation of 26 August 1606
sources: AGS, CC, leg. 934, transcribed in López Rodríguez (2023), pp.166-167

stops.name: Madrid, ten months at court
stops.date_confidence: attested, endorsed 12 May 1607 (AGS, CC, leg. 926, transcribed in López Rodríguez 2023, p.168)
stops.campa: She asks for the office of escribano de las entradas of the Cárcel de la Corte, the clerkship that registers prisoners into the court prison of Madrid, to help defray what the suit is costing her. She has been ten months at court, she says, pursuing the alguacilazgo, and is muy gastada y empeñada, heavily spent and in debt. She is somewhere near fifty years old, in lodgings in a city not her own, spending money she does not have on the prospect of an office.
suggested_refs: AGS, Cámara de Castilla, legajo 926
sources: AGS, CC, leg. 926, transcribed in López Rodríguez (2023), p.168

stops.name: Madrid, the goods of three dead clerics
stops.date_confidence: attested, document dated 2 July 1607 (AGS, CC, leg. 917, transcribed in López Rodríguez 2023, pp.168-169)
stops.campa: Three clerics have died in Galicia, Pedro Yáñez of San Pedro de Lodoña, Gutierre Gómez and Enrique Estévez, and their goods have reverted to the Cámara Real for want of heirs. She petitions to be given them. The request has nothing whatever to do with the siege, and she attaches the siege to it anyway, because the siege is the only capital she has, and every petition she writes for fifty years is drawn on that one account. The paper is in Cámara de Castilla, legajo 917.
suggested_refs: AGS, Cámara de Castilla, legajo 917
sources: AGS, CC, leg. 917, transcribed in López Rodríguez (2023), pp.168-169

stops.name: El Pardo, the order sent a second time
stops.date_confidence: attested, cédula issued at El Pardo 28 January 1608 (AGS, Libros de Guerra no.105, transcribed in full in López Rodríguez 2023, p.165)
stops.campa: At El Pardo, the hunting palace north of Madrid, a cédula is issued to Don Diego de las Mariñas, governor of Galicia, ordering him to carry out the earlier order exempting her house from billeting, which he has not carried out. Twelve years have passed since the first order. The king writes to Galicia; Galicia does not answer; the king writes again, and she is standing in Madrid to make him write it. It is the last document of hers that the court registers. The register is the Libros de Guerra, number 105.
suggested_refs: AGS, Libros de Guerra, no. 105
sources: AGS, Libros de Guerra, no.105, transcribed in López Rodríguez (2023), p.165

stops.name: Sigrás, Cambre, widowed a fourth time
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year (López Rodríguez 2023 p.158; Briante Benítez 2020 p.106); month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinates are the Sigrás parish seat, 43°17'21"N 8°21'38"O
stops.campa: Gil Bermúdez de Figueroa dies and she is a widow for the fourth time, and this time she is a landowner. The property is at Sigrás, in the parish of Cambre, inland from A Coruña up the valley: fields under grain, vines, farm buildings, and the standing of a woman who holds land in her own hand and answers to no husband about it. She is about sixty. The remarriage clause in Gil's will costs her nothing in the end, because she does not marry again, and she stays on the land at Sigrás for thirty years.
suggested_refs: The Pita holdings in the parish of Santiago de Sigrás, Cambre

stops.name: Sigrás, the wine going down to the city
stops.date_confidence: attested as a description of her later years (López Rodríguez 2023, p.158) rather than as a dated event; 1615 is an ordering date within the widowhood that begins in 1613
stops.campa: She farms the land at Sigrás and sells what it makes. She harvests wheat. She lends money at interest. Grain, vines, casks, debts and the suits that come out of them: this is what the notarial record of her actually contains for the last thirty years of her life, and it is the part that no play and no bronze has ever wanted. The wine goes down to A Coruña in pipes, sold to the taverners of the city, and with at least one taverner she ends in court over the account.
suggested_refs: Notarial instruments of the Sigrás years: wine sales, loans and the resulting suits

stops.name: A Coruña, her name in verse inside a lawsuit
stops.date_confidence: attested to a span, 1616-1619, the years of the Real Audiencia case; the exact year of the folio is not fixed, and 1616 is the opening of the span. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Martín de Cavalar sues her over the holding of Ledoño before the Real Audiencia de Galicia, and inside the file, on folio seventeen, somebody has copied out a set of verses in Galician that begin María Pita está remendada. They are mocking, or teasing, or simply local; they involve a fire in the night and the Pelamios going off to dance. While she is alive and litigating, her name is already something people put into rhyme, a century and a half before the heroic ballads. Whether the folio was copied into the file to insult her or to amuse the clerk, the record does not say.
stops.quote: María Pita esta remendada / Que tubo mui gran desgracia / a noite do lume / se oubera de queimar sin sanar. / Y o maldito de Cavalar / a yl y a Panpin os Pelamios / ban a bailar...
stops.quote_source: Real Audiencia de Galicia, Martín de Cavalar con Maior Fernández Pita de Cámara, auto ordinario sobre o lugar de Ledoño, 1616-1619, fol. 17, transcribed by María del Pilar Rodríguez Suárez in Saavedra Vázquez, María Pita: una aproximación a su vida y a su tiempo (2003), p.226
suggested_refs: The Cavalar suit over Ledoño, Real Audiencia de Galicia, 1616-1619

stops.name: A Coruña, counting the lawsuits
stops.date_confidence: the count covers her whole adult life and is not an event; 1620 is an ordering date. The figure itself is contested: Briante Benítez (2020) p.106 itemises twenty-seven, López Rodríguez (2023) p.173 says about twenty. The figure of thirty-five that circulates could not be traced to any source
stops.campa: Counting her lawsuits is itself a scholarly disagreement. Briante Benítez, following Saavedra Vázquez, itemises twenty-seven; López Rodríguez, working the same archive, says about a score. Property, debt, insult, violence, family right. She sues her son-in-law, her taverners and her neighbours, is prosecuted in turn, and is sentenced at least once to exile from the city she is famous for defending. Of Briante's twenty-seven, sixteen are criminal querellas, nine brought by her and seven against her.
suggested_refs: The itemised case list in Martínez Salazar 1988, pp.237-240

stops.name: A Coruña, what the crown actually pays
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. What is documented is five escudos a month with an alférez's pay attached (López Rodríguez 2023, pp.163, 175). The 1633 notarial instrument said to record ten escudos a month could not be traced to a citable archival reference by any route available here; the figure is reported and left unconfirmed. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: What the crown pays her, by the documents that can be followed, is five escudos a month with the pay of an alférez attached to it. A notarial instrument of 1633, drawn when she is very old and again a widow, is reported to record ten escudos a month, which would mean the stipend doubled at some point in the intervening years. Nobody citing that instrument has produced its reference. Either she was paid twice what the petitions asked for, or the number is a copy of a copy. The record as it stands does not settle it.
suggested_refs: Early seventeenth-century documentation at arquivosdegalicia.xunta.gal
sources: Arquivos de Galicia, early-17th-century documentation (untraced for the 1633 figure)

stops.name: Sigrás, Cambre, she died suddenly
stops.date_confidence: attested, the burial entry of the parish of Santiago de Sigrás, found by Xosé Antón García Ledo in the Archivo Histórico Diocesano de Santiago (López Rodríguez 2023, pp.171-173)
stops.campa: She dies suddenly at Sigrás on the twenty-first of February, 1643, an old woman of eighty-odd years by one reckoning of her birth and seventy-five by another. The entry calls her Mayor Fernández Pita, the name she was born with and the name the notaries always used, and not the name she signed to kings. The parish burial book of Santiago de Sigrás records the death in a single clause, naming no illness, no accident and no last rites: se murio Mayor Fernandez Pita de repente.
stops.quote: se murio Mayor Fernandez Pita de repente
stops.quote_source: Burial book of the parish of Santiago de Sigrás, Cambre, 21 February 1643, Archivo Histórico Diocesano de Santiago, quoted in López Rodríguez (2023), p.172
suggested_refs: The burial book of Santiago de Sigrás, Cambre
sources: García Ledo / Bardos Cultural and the Museo Arqueolóxico de Cambre on the unresolved grave

stops.name: Convento de Santo Domingo, the grave that was never found
stops.date_confidence: the testamentary request is quoted verbatim in the burial entry of 21 February 1643; that the request was not honoured, and that no grave has been identified, is stated by López Rodríguez (2023) pp.172-173. The date here is the day after the death, used to order the segment
stops.campa: Her will asks for burial at Santo Domingo in A Coruña, the Dominican house the English had used as a gun position in the week her second husband was killed, and it asks for a place beside her fourth husband. The parish of Sigrás does not send the body. The burial entry copies out the request and then the record stops. No grave of hers has been identified at Sigrás, at Santo Domingo, or anywhere else. The city that will take her for its emblem does not know where she is.
stops.quote: tenia echo testamento por el qual semando enterrar en santo Domingo dela ciudad dela Coruna
stops.quote_source: Burial entry of Mayor Fernández Pita, parish of Santiago de Sigrás, 21 February 1643, quoted in López Rodríguez (2023), p.172
suggested_refs: The convent of Santo Domingo, A Coruña, named in her testament

stops.name: The breach, a cry with no witness
stops.date_confidence: the stop sits at the breach because the words are attributed to that place; the date is that of the earliest located attestation, Feijoo's Teatro crítico universal, Tomo I, Discurso XVI (1726), 137 years after the siege. Note that López Rodríguez p.174 misnumbers this as the sixth discourse. No 1589 source contains the cry. The Galician wording 'Quen teña honra, que me siga' is later still, and its first appearance is not fixed here
stops.campa: The words everybody knows, whoever has honour, follow me, appear in no account of the siege written by anyone who was at the siege. The earliest text yet found that puts a cry in her mouth is Benito Jerónimo Feijoo's Defensa de las mujeres, printed in 1726, where she snatches a sword and buckler out of a soldier's hands, reproaches the men with their cowardice and throws herself into the breach. That is a hundred and thirty-seven years after the breach was made.
stops.quote: una María Pita [...] exprobó a los nuestros su cobardía arrancando espada y rodela de las manos de un soldado y clamando que quien tuviese honra la siguiese, encendida en coraje se arrojó a la brecha.
stops.quote_source: Benito Jerónimo Feijoo, Teatro crítico universal, Tomo I, Discurso XVI, 'Defensa de las mujeres' (1726), quoted in López Rodríguez (2023), p.174
suggested_refs: Feijoo, Teatro crítico universal, Tomo I, Discurso XVI, 'Defensa de las mujeres' (1726)
sources: Xulia Cabaleiro, 'María Pita: a xénese dun mito,' Festa da palabra silenciada 7 (1990)

stops.name: A Coruña, the heroine raised in rank
stops.date_confidence: posthumous reception, dated by publication. Valladares de Sotomayor's comedy is of 1784 and was staged in Madrid; Robello y Vasconi's drama is of 1833 and was written in A Coruña. The stop is pinned to her own city, not to a theatre she never entered. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: On the stage she rises in class. Antonio Valladares de Sotomayor's comedy of 1784 wraps the siege around an invented love plot and makes her single and well born, a governor's daughter, because heroic drama of that period does not know what to do with a shopkeeper's daughter twice married to butchers. Francisco Robello y Vasconi, an actor of the A Coruña company, writes a closer version in 1833 and still gets the detail wrong: his Rocamonde is a baker, and his María Pita has an aged mother to protect in 1589, six years after her mother died.
suggested_refs: Valladares de Sotomayor, Defensa de La Coruña por la heroica María Pita (1784); Robello y Vasconi, María Pita o la heroína de Galicia (1833), BNE MSS/17427

stops.name: A Coruña, the archive opened and a face invented
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of publication of El cerco de La Coruña en 1589 y Mayor Fernández Pita; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Andrés Martínez Salazar publishes El cerco de La Coruña en 1589 y Mayor Fernández Pita, goes into the archives, prints the sentences and the petitions, and recovers the documented woman for the first time. In the same book he supplies what the archive does not hold, a body and a face: she must have been of tall stature and of no common beauty. No portrait made from life exists. Everything the nineteenth century put on canvas descends from a sentence a scholar wrote about a woman he had never seen.
stops.quote: debió ser de estatura elevada y de nada vulgar belleza
stops.quote_source: Andrés Martínez Salazar, El cerco de La Coruña en 1589 y Mayor Fernández Pita (1889), quoted in López Rodríguez (2023), p.174
suggested_refs: Martínez Salazar, El cerco de La Coruña en 1589 y Mayor Fernández Pita (1889), archive.org/details/elcercodelacoru00salagoog
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'María Pita', on the absence of a portrait from life

stops.name: Praza de María Pita, the bronze
stops.date_confidence: 1998 per es.wikipedia 'Plaza de María Pita' and gl.wikipedia 'Monumento a María Pita'. The 1968 date given in the caption of López Rodríguez (2023) p.155 is a typographical error and is not followed here. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: In the square that carries her name, in front of the city hall of A Coruña, a bronze by José Castiñeiras Iglesias is set up: the figure three metres and a third, the pedestal five and a half, thirty tonnes standing better than nine metres above the paving. She holds the pike. Xulia Cabaleiro's argument, made eight years before the statue, is that the nineteenth century took the collective action of many women at the wall and pressed it into one exceptional woman, masculinised for a single afternoon to make her fit for history.
suggested_refs: The monument to María Pita by José Castiñeiras Iglesias, Praza de María Pita, A Coruña
sources: Xulia Cabaleiro, 'María Pita: a xénese dun mito,' Festa da palabra silenciada 7 (1990), pp.99-100, cited in López Rodríguez (2023), p.175
